1.explanation: The root cause of the issue is in the render method of the RadioButton class in the 'packages/react/src/components/RadioButton/RadioButton.js' file. The code sets the aria-label attribute on the <label> element, which is unnecessary and may actually prevent screen readers from accessing the label text via the standard association of <input> and <label> (using the for and id attributes). As a result, the screen reader does not announce the label as it should. To fix the bug, the render method should be edited to remove the aria-label attribute from the <label> element, restoring the expected accessibility behavior.
1.bug_scenario: The bug scenario involves a screen reader (such as VoiceOver or JAWS) not reading the label of a radio button in the React implementation of the Carbon Design System. In the vanilla HTML version, the screen reader reads the label correctly, but in the React version, the label is not announced. The bug report and images show that in the React version, the <label> tag includes an unnecessary aria-label attribute, which may interfere with the screen reader's ability to announce the label text as expected.

2.explanation: The core accessibility bug is rooted in how the React RadioButton component renders its label. In the compressed file, the 'RadioButton' class and its 'render' method are responsible for outputting the <label> and <input> elements. The bug relates to setting the 'aria-label' attribute on the <label> element, which is unnecessary and may interfere with how assistive technologies interpret and announce the label. Instead, the label text should be placed as content inside the <label> element, matching the vanilla HTML structure. Thus, the key bug elements are the 'RadioButton' class and its 'render' function, which directly control the markup and ARIA attributes affecting screen reader behavior.
2.bug_scenario: The bug scenario is that when using a screen reader (such as VoiceOver or JAWS) on the React implementation of the Carbon Design System's RadioButton component, the screen reader does not read the radio button label as expected, in contrast to the vanilla HTML version. This makes the component inaccessible for users relying on assistive technologies. The provided images show the difference in what is read aloud: the vanilla version correctly reads the label, while the React version omits it or reads only part of it, likely due to incorrect use of the aria-label attribute on the <label> element.
